lead.headline: Texas Pacific Land agrees to buy EagleRock for about $3 billion in stock to widen its Permian water platform
lead.dek: The all-stock deal adds 59,000 acres in Lea County, New Mexico and Midland Basin water assets, lifting combined sourcing and treatment capacity to about 1.5 million barrels a day.
body: Texas Pacific Land said on November 23 it will acquire EagleRock Land in an all-stock deal with an implied equity value of about $3 billion. EagleRock holders get 0.0831 shares of a new TPL holding company for each Class A share, about $23.56 based on TPL's five-day average price to November 20. TPL holders will own about 86% of the combined company. Reuters reported EagleRock shares up about 16% before the open.

Water is a large part of the logic. EagleRock brings about 220,000 barrels a day of produced water handling across gathering, disposal and recycling, plus about 130,000 barrels a day of non-potable supply, much of it tied to long-term arrangements with Double Eagle covering about 105,000 dedicated acres. Combined, TPL would have about 1.5 million barrels a day of non-potable sourcing and produced water treatment, up 49%, and about 68 million barrels of storage, up 79%.

The deal also adds about 59,000 fee-owned acres, mostly in Lea County, which the companies say accounts for about 25% of Permian horizontal well permits and 20% of completion water demand. Chief executive Tyler Glover said it reinforces a "high-margin, capital-light business model." Closing is expected in the first half of 2027, subject to an EagleRock shareholder vote and antitrust clearance; holders of more than 50% of EagleRock's voting power have agreed to support it.

use.text: Fewer, larger water landlords in the Permian mean longer contracts and less room to bargain.
Land plus water carries high margins: about 83% pro forma adjusted EBITDA margin this year.
After Deep Blue and Pilot, this is the third big Permian water deal in a month.
More produced water in fewer hands puts disposal and pore space rules at the center.

briefs.headline: California Water Service places $275 million of debt a week before becoming Watermark Utilities
briefs.text: California Water Service Group said on November 23 it finalized private placements of $125 million of senior unsecured notes, at 6.08% due 2031 and 6.41% due 2036, and its Cal Water subsidiary sold $150 million of first mortgage bonds at 6.49% due 2046 and 6.54% due 2056. Proceeds will refinance existing debt and fund general corporate purposes. The group serves more than 2.2 million people in five states and takes the name Watermark Utilities on November 30.
briefs.why: Long dated utility debt is pricing above 6%, a cost that flows into future rate cases. The company's own risk factors list the EPA PFAS limits and their legal challenges.

briefs.headline: UN General Assembly agrees to hold a water conference every three years from 2031
briefs.text: The General Assembly adopted by consensus on November 23 a resolution led by the UAE and Senegal that sets periodic UN water conferences, with governments meeting every three years from 2031 after the agreed 2026 and 2028 meetings. The 2026 conference runs December 8 to 10 in Abu Dhabi, the first devoted to the sanitation and water goal, SDG 6. Before 2023, the UN had not held one since 1977.
briefs.why: A fixed cycle gives water a standing place on the global agenda. About 2.1 billion people still lacked safely managed drinking water in 2024, and the World Bank puts the scarcity cost to the Middle East and North Africa at 6 to 14% of GDP by 2050.

briefs.headline: Satellite images show river diversion under way at China's 60 GW Yarlung Tsangpo dam near India
briefs.text: Business Today, citing a Times of India report based on EarthSense Labs imagery, said on November 24 that villages at the proposed Mainling site were cleared by December 2025 and that river diversion works, roads and housing appeared by August 2026. The Medog project, estimated at 1.2 trillion yuan, about $168 billion, is planned as five cascade stations on the river that becomes the Siang in India. India's proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper project, with a reservoir of about 9.2 billion cubic meters, faces local opposition over displacement.
briefs.why: There is no binding water sharing treaty between the two countries, so the Brahmaputra basin is one of the largest transboundary water risks in Asia.

briefs.headline: Free cyber defense for rural water utilities now reaches 26 states
briefs.text: The Water Watch Center, launched in August by the National Rural Water Association and the volunteer group DEF CON Franklin, pays security firms including Rapid7 and BlastWave to give small utilities free intrusion detection and consultations. It said utilities in 26 states are now covered and nearly 100 have reached out. Funders include Craig Newmark Philanthropies, the Hewlett Foundation and DARPA.
briefs.why: Iran linked hackers breached water systems in several US states this summer, and most small utilities have no security staff.

briefs.headline: San Antonio eases to Stage 2 watering rules as the Edwards Aquifer recovers
briefs.text: San Antonio Water System said on November 23 it is moving from Stage 3 to Stage 2 restrictions after the Edwards Aquifer's 10-day average rose above the 640 foot Stage 3 trigger. Drought surcharges on single family use above 20,000 gallons a month end, and lawn watering stays limited to once a week by address.
briefs.why: Drought surcharges are a real revenue line for Texas utilities, and their end shows how quickly aquifer levels can swing rate and demand planning.

company.name: VA Tech Wabag
company.headline: Wabag's order book passed ₹20,000 crore, then Saudi Arabia pulled a big one
company.body: The Chennai based water treatment and desalination contractor reported first half revenue up 20% to about ₹1,887 crore and net profit up 29% to about ₹195 crore for the period to September 30, with net cash for a 15th straight quarter. Chairman and managing director Rajiv Mittal pointed to two large desalination orders, a seawater plant in Kuwait and a plant at Jamnagar in India. Management said revenue growth could reach the top of its 15% to 20% guidance. Nine days later the Saudi Water Authority cancelled the 300,000 cubic meter a day Yanbu award, and the company said it is seeking the reasons before deciding next steps.

leader.name: Estelle Brachlianoff
leader.body: Brachlianoff has run Veolia since July 2022, and shareholders renewed her board seat in April 2026 through the 2030 annual meeting. Her GreenUp plan leans on water technology and hazardous waste: Veolia agreed to buy US hazardous waste company Clean Earth for about $3 billion, won two Mumbai water projects in February and launched an integrated offer for data centers.

supplier.name: Ecolab
supplier.headline: Ecolab's water business is being pulled by chips and AI data centers
body: Ecolab reported third quarter sales up 13% to $4.69 billion on October 27, with organic growth accelerating to 7%. Chairman and chief executive Christophe Beck called the quarter an inflection point, and the water segment is where the change shows most clearly.

Global Water sales rose 20% at fixed currency to $2.48 billion. Eleven points came from the Ovivo Electronics and CoolIT acquisitions, and the rest from organic growth led by Global High-Tech, which grew 63% organically on semiconductor and data center demand.

The cost of that bet is visible too. CoolIT amortization and financing took roughly 10% off adjusted earnings growth, holding adjusted EPS to $2.18, up 5%. Management guides full-year adjusted EPS to $8.10 to $8.20.
supplier.why: Fabs and hyperscale data centers now set the pace for industrial water treatment. Expect bundled water, cooling and digital contracts and tighter supply of ultrapure water expertise.

innovation.name: Claros Technologies
innovation.headline: Claros takes PFAS destruction to full scale at Daikin
innovation.body: Most PFAS treatment moves the chemicals into another waste stream. Claros breaks them apart with its ClarosTechUV system. On October 1 it signed a commercial agreement with Daikin America for full-scale deployment at Daikin's plant in Decatur, Alabama, after a December 2025 run treated more than 170,000 gallons of process water with greater than 99.99% destruction of target PFAS.

investor.name: Burnt Island Ventures
investor.headline: The most active water-only venture firm
investor.body: Founded in New York by water industry veteran Tom Ferguson, Burnt Island invests only in early stage water technology. Xylem anchored both of its funds, with climate fund of funds WovenEarth Ventures joining Fund II. Published deal trackers show 2026 investments in Aquatic Labs, Crew Carbon, Biota and Verdi.

capital.intro: Private equity has executed 435 water deals across 25 countries since 2015 and more than doubled its holdings since 2019, according to Bluefield Research. Most of those assets are under three years old, which points to an exit wave.

firm.body: XPV invests only in water and builds platforms through add-on acquisitions. In June it exited Axius Water alongside co-owner KKR. Founding partner David Henderson leads the firm.

security.headline: The UN says the world has entered water bankruptcy
security.text: A UN University report in January argued that groundwater depletion, overallocation and pollution have pushed many basins past the point of recovery, and that "crisis" no longer describes it.

security.headline: The US and Mexico set Colorado River rules for 2027 and 2028
security.text: The two countries signed a formal agreement in September on new operating guidelines for the river that supplies seven US states and northern Mexico.

security.headline: The Gulf runs on desalination
security.text: The Middle East and North Africa host over 40% of global desalination capacity, and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries alone hold 33%.

place.name: Basilica Cistern
place.headline: A sixth century reservoir held up by a forest of 336 columns
body: Built between 532 and 542 under the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian I, the Basilica Cistern, Yerebatan Sarnıcı in Turkish, was one of the city's major water stores, with an estimated capacity of about 100,000 tons. Its roof rests on 336 columns, each 9 meters tall.

Two carved Medusa heads, identified in 1986, serve as column bases, one upside down and one on its side. The cistern opened to visitors in 1987 after a major restoration, and reopened on July 22, 2022 after a second restoration that began in 2014.
place.visit: In Istanbul's historic peninsula; open as a museum. Check opening hours and tickets before you go.
place.why: Istanbul hosts the IWRA World Water Congress in October 2027, and this is the city's oldest lesson in storing water close to demand.
